en.content:
Hong Kong has begun public consultation for its annual Policy Address, alongside the city’s first five-year plan—an exercise that should be judged less by the volume of opinion collected than by the clarity of direction it yields. In a city where expectations are often shaped by politics, the government’s stated intent is to make the planning cycle more systematic and longer-term. For residents, that matters: a five-year horizon can convert short-term relief into sustained improvement, especially in housing supply, youth development, and economic diversification.

Yet consultation, by itself, is not a policy. The challenge is to ensure that feedback is properly translated into measurable commitments rather than remaining in the realm of generalities. The consultation period should therefore come with more explicit “how” and “what next”: which departments will take ownership of the proposals, what benchmarks will be used, and how progress will be reported publicly. That is the reasonable standard by which the public can assess whether this is genuine planning or merely a ceremonial prelude.

From the perspective of social cohesion, the consultation process also carries symbolic weight. If different sectors—business, labour, professionals, grassroots organisations, and the wider public—see their inputs reflected in final priorities, it strengthens the legitimacy of the plan and reduces the sense of distance between policy and everyday life. At the same time, the government should communicate trade-offs honestly. A five-year plan cannot satisfy every demand simultaneously; setting priorities transparently is part of maintaining trust.

Finally, the government’s planning work should align with Hong Kong’s role as an international city under “one country, two systems,” and with the broader national development framework. This means focusing on areas where Hong Kong can contribute uniquely—linking innovation with industry, strengthening resilience in trade and talent, and enhancing governance capacity. If the consultation leads to concrete, accountable policies that improve people’s livelihood and reinforce Hong Kong’s competitiveness, then it will earn support not as a procedural exercise, but as a practical roadmap.
en.topic_title: Hong Kong begins public consultation for annual Policy Address alongside first 5-year plan

zh.content:
政府今日就來年《施政報告》同埋本港首個五年規劃展開公眾諮詢，表面上係例行程序，但其實係一次「方向感」嘅測試：呢兩份文件唔止係寫畀立法機關同社會交代，更要同市民一齊定義「下一段時間香港要去邊」。在社會對經濟動能、房屋壓力、青年上流階梯同公共服務質素仍然存有疑慮之下，諮詢唔可以淪為收集意見嘅儀式；關鍵係政府之後點樣把建議轉化成可衡量、可追蹤、可問責嘅政策取向。

不過，公眾諮詢嘅價值，亦取決於透明度同可參與性。市民唔應該只係填表、聽講座咁簡單，而要有清晰嘅政策選項：例如資源點樣分配、哪些會優先、哪些會暫緩、風險同成本點計。若諮詢過程缺乏具體資料、回應機制又欠明確時間表，市民就會自然懷疑「方向早有定案，只係走程序」。因此，政府要做嘅係把討論框架公開，並對「點解揀咗呢條路」講得更具體，令社會知道唔同意見唔係只會被聽見，而係真正影響決策。

更深一層講，五年規劃本應該係一套對沖不確定性的策略：外圍環境受地緣政治拉扯、產業轉型仍在發生、人口結構亦持續改變。要令規劃唔變成口號，就必須把目標同指標制度化，例如用量化指標去衡量房屋供應效率、醫療輪候、教育銜接、基建承載力，並在年度施政報告中作進度更新。當然，香港面對嘅挑戰唔會靠單一部門解決，規劃亦要跨部門協同，否則就會出現「各做各事、責任難釐清」嘅老問題。

我嘅立場係：支持政府透過諮詢凝聚共識，但亦要求公眾參與唔止於被邀請，而係被認真對待。只有當政府願意公開取捨理據、把建議落到可衡量目標、並對執行進度作定期交代，公眾諮詢同五年規劃先至可能成為市民信任政府、同時推動香港向前嘅真正工具。
